content: Uterine fibroids are the most common benign tumors found in women of reproductive age. These growths are often associated with symptoms such as heavy menstrual bleeding and difficulties with fertility. Many women turn to herbal preparations as an alternative to surgical interventions for managing these fibroids. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness and safety of Chinese herbal medicine in treating uterine fibroids. To achieve this, the authors conducted a comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Trials Register, the Cochrane Complementary Medicine Field Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Chinese Biomedical Database, TCMLARS, AMED, and LILACS. The search was completed on September 11, 2012. The study included randomized controlled trials that compared herbal preparations to no treatment, placebo, medical therapies, or surgical procedures in women diagnosed with uterine fibroids. Trials that combined herbal preparations with conventional therapies were also included. Data collection and analysis were performed independently by two reviewers, who assessed the risk of bias in the trials. Dichotomous data were presented as risk ratios (RR), while continuous outcomes were expressed as mean differences (MD), both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A total of 21 randomized trials involving 2,222 women were included in the analysis. However, most of these trials were found to have either unclear or high risk of bias. The herbal preparations used in the trials varied widely, and the average treatment duration ranged from three to six months. Notably, none of the included trials reported on the primary outcome of uterine fibroid-related symptoms. Instead, most trials focused on secondary outcomes such as fibroid volume and uterine size. When compared to mifepristone, the extract of Tripterygium wilfordii was associated with a greater reduction in fibroid volume (MD -23.03 cm³, 95% CI -28.39 to -17.67; 2 trials) and uterine size (MD -51.25 cm³, 95% CI -77.70 to -24.80; 2 trials). On the other hand, there was no significant difference observed between the herbal product Nona Roguy and gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists in terms of average fibroid volume or uterine size. However, the combination of the Guizhi Fuling formula with mifepristone resulted in a greater reduction in fibroid volume (MD -1.72, 95% CI -2.42 to -1.02; 7 trials) and uterine size (MD -31.63, 95% CI -54.58 to -8.68; 3 trials) compared to mifepristone alone. Adverse events were reported in 13 out of the 21 trials, but no serious adverse effects related to the use of herbal preparations were documented. The authors concluded that the current evidence is insufficient to either support or refute the use of herbal preparations for the treatment of uterine fibroids. This is due to the limited number of high-quality studies with large sample sizes. They emphasized the need for further well-designed trials that evaluate clinically relevant outcomes.
